title: Fermi + decision: public DC fast-charging ports for 2030
notes: Reference chain (central): 245k households x 1.7 = ~416k vehicles; x 12% EV = ~50k EVs. No home charging 30% = ~15k EVs x (200 mi x 70% / 150 mi) = ~0.93 sessions/wk = ~14k/wk. Home chargers ~35k x ~0.46/wk (2/month) = ~16k/wk. Fleet 1,500 x 5 = 7.5k/wk. Total ~38k sessions/wk = ~5.4k/day. Port capacity at 25% x 24 h = 360 min / 40 min = 9 sessions/day -> ~600 ports (low inputs ~430, high ~780; ~550 new after the existing 46). $12M / $140k-$220k = ~55-86 ports, i.e. roughly 10-15% of the need.

decision_paraphrases: No - $12M buys roughly 55-85 ports, about 10-15% of the ~600 needed.
Not enough: it covers only a small share of the need.
$12M is insufficient; it funds about 12% of required ports.
decision_negatives: Yes, $12M is enough to meet 2030 demand.

items.text: EV count: households x vehicles per household x EV share (8-16%) gives ~33k-67k EVs
paraphrases: EVs in 2030: 245k households x 1.7 = 416k vehicles; at 12% EV share that's about 50,000 EVs.
EV adoption of 8-16% gives 33k to 67k EVs.
Number of EVs = vehicles x EV share.

items.text: Home-charging access: 25-35% of EV owners lack home charging and depend on public fast charging
paraphrases: 30% of EV owners lack home charging: about 15,000 drivers depend on public chargers.
Share without home charging (25-35%) is a key driver.
Apartment dwellers and street parkers rely on fast charging.

items.text: Session frequency: 200 mi/week x 70% from DC fast / 150 mi per session = ~0.9 sessions/week for drivers without home charging
paraphrases: 200 miles x 70% / 150 miles = 0.93 fast-charge sessions per week per driver without home charging.
Each no-home-charging EV needs about 0.9 sessions a week.
Charging frequency from weekly miles and miles per session.

items.text: Drivers with home charging still add substantial load: ~2 sessions/month x the majority of EVs (~16k sessions/week, comparable to the no-home group)
paraphrases: Drivers with home charging still use DC fast chargers twice a month: 35k x 0.46 = ~16k sessions a week.
Home-charging owners add occasional sessions (2 per month) that are a large share of total demand.
Don't ignore occasional fast charging by drivers with home charging.

items.text: Ride-hail and delivery fleets: 1,500 EVs x 5 sessions/week = 7,500 sessions/week
paraphrases: Fleets: 1,500 EVs x 5 sessions a week = 7,500 sessions.
Ride-hail and delivery vehicles add about 7.5k sessions per week.
Fleet charging is a large, concentrated load.

items.text: Port throughput: 25% of 24 h = 6 h = 360 min / 40 min = ~9 sessions per port per day
paraphrases: Each port handles about 9 sessions a day at 25% utilization (360 minutes / 40 minutes).
Utilization cap of 25% limits throughput per port.
Port capacity = 6 usable hours per day.
Subtract the 46 existing ports from the total need.
The city already has 46 ports, so new ports needed are about 550.
Existing chargers cover a small part.

items.text: Budget arithmetic: $12M / $140k-$220k = ~55-86 ports, a small fraction of the need
paraphrases: $12M buys about 55-86 ports at $140k-$220k each.
Budget covers about 67 ports at $180k per port.
With the budget we can fund roughly 60-85 ports.

items.text: Leverage other sources: private charging operators, utilities, grants, and cheaper Level 2 / workplace charging
paraphrases: Leverage private charging operators and utility programs; the city can't fund it alone.
Use cheaper Level 2 and workplace charging where possible.
Public-private partnerships and grants should fill the gap.

items.text: Phase and target: put first ports where residents lack home charging; build in stages and revisit as adoption becomes clearer
paraphrases: Phase the build-out and revisit annually as adoption becomes clear.
Target the first ports to neighborhoods where residents lack home charging.
Build in stages and monitor utilization before expanding.
